summary:
Cabin Vitals is a web-based astronaut health monitoring and self-guidance system developed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. We developed an interactive dashboard that allows astronauts to record and monitor seven health indicators: blood pressure, resting heart rate, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep duration, mood, and countermeasure exercise.
The system follows a simple Log – Assess – Act – Share process. It evaluates health readings, displays Normal, Watch, or Alert statuses, provides interactive body maps and health trend charts, and offers guidance on the actions to take. It also generates a flight surgeon note that astronauts can review and share.

Cabin Vitals addresses the challenge of maintaining astronaut health during space exploration by considering the five major hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile closed environments. It also considers communication delays, particularly during Mars missions, where immediate assistance from Earth may not be possible.
This project is important because astronauts need a simple way to understand their health and recognize potential concerns while living and working in challenging space environments. By encouraging regular health monitoring, early awareness, and informed action, Cabin Vitals aims to support astronaut well-being and contribute to safer, longer-duration human space missions.
details:
1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Cabin Vitals is a web-based astronaut health monitoring and self-guidance system designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. It helps astronauts monitor their physical and mental well-being, understand changes in their health, and decide what action to take.

The system monitors seven important health indicators:

  • Blood pressure
  • Resting heart rate
  • Blood glucose
  • Body temperature
  • Sleep duration
  • Mood
  • Countermeasure exercise

It works through a simple four-step process:

  1. Log: Astronauts enter their daily health measurements.
  2. Assess: The system evaluates the measurements and displays their status as Normal, Watch, or Alert.
  3. Act: It provides simple instructions and recommended actions based on the recorded values.
  4. Share: It generates a flight surgeon note containing health readings, trends, and flagged indicators, which astronauts can review and share through their normal communication channel.

The system also provides interactive body maps, health trend charts, measurement guides, and reminders to encourage regular health monitoring. It supports different mission environments, including space stations, lunar bases, Mars transit, and the Mars surface.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Helps astronauts monitor their physical and mental health regularly.
  • Identifies unusual health readings and changes in health trends.
  • Provides clear guidance without requiring astronauts to have medical expertise.
  • Encourages daily health checks through reminders, experience points, levels, streaks, and badges.
  • Helps astronauts understand how spaceflight hazards may affect their health.
  • Supports communication with flight surgeons through a prepared health summary.
  • Considers communication delays during deep-space missions by providing guidance for different mission environments.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The main aim of Cabin Vitals is to improve astronaut health awareness and encourage early recognition of potential health problems during long-duration space missions.

On missions to the Moon and Mars, astronauts may experience communication delays and limited access to immediate medical assistance. Cabin Vitals aims to help crew members take a more active role in monitoring their own health while following clear guidance on when to inform the crew or contact a flight surgeon.

In the future, the project could support safer and more sustainable human space exploration by encouraging preventive health monitoring and better communication between astronauts and medical teams on Earth.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

The project was developed as a web-based software prototype using:

  • HTML: To structure the application's interface and content.
  • CSS: To design the layout, dashboard, colors, charts, and responsive interface.
  • JavaScript: To implement health calculations, status assessment, interactive body maps, trend charts, reminders, and report generation.

The prototype runs through a web browser and does not currently require dedicated hardware or external medical sensors. Health measurements are entered manually by the user.

5. How is the project creative?

Cabin Vitals combines health monitoring, interactive visualization, and self-guidance in one system.

Its creative features include:

  • An interactive human body map that allows users to select health indicators and view their status.
  • A three-level health status system using green, amber, and red colors, paired with different shapes for accessibility.
  • Dynamic charts that help astronauts understand health changes over time.
  • A hazard-based view that connects health indicators with the five major hazards of human spaceflight.
  • Gamification features such as XP, levels, streaks, and badges to encourage consistent health monitoring.
  • Mission-specific guidance that considers the communication delay between Earth and different space environments.
  • Automatic generation of a flight surgeon note for review and sharing.

These features make health information easier to understand and turn daily measurements into practical next steps.

6. What factors did the team consider?

While developing Cabin Vitals, the team considered several important factors:

  • Spaceflight hazards: Radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile closed environments.
  • Physical and mental health: Both physical measurements and psychological well-being, including mood and sleep.
  • Communication delays: The time required to communicate with Earth, especially during Mars missions.
  • Ease of use: A simple and understandable interface suitable for astronauts who are not medical professionals.
  • Early awareness: Identifying unusual readings and health trends before they become more serious.
  • Accessibility: Using colors together with shapes so that status information is not communicated through color alone.
  • Consistency: Encouraging regular measurements through reminders and gamification.
  • Safety and limitations: The prototype uses illustrative example data and simplified adult reference ranges. It is designed for educational demonstration and is not a certified medical device.

Conclusion

Cabin Vitals is a practical software concept that aims to make astronaut health monitoring simpler, more interactive, and more accessible. By combining daily health tracking, visual assessment, personalized guidance, and flight surgeon report generation, the project encourages astronauts to take an active role in their health during long-duration space missions. It has the potential to be further developed into a more advanced astronaut health support system.
